results.title: External validation or a bigger modelling sample? - data analysis / model validation - Datamethods Discussion Forum
results.content: This is a place where statisticians, epidemiologists, informaticists, machine learning practitioners, and other research methodologists communicate with themselves and with clinical, translational, and health services researchers to discuss issues related to data: research methods, quantitative methods, study design, measurement, statistical analysis, interpretation of data and statistical results, clinical trials, journal articles, statistical graphics, causal inference, medical decision making, and more. # External validation or a bigger modelling sample? I have 920 cases from my institution, but I am concerned about external validation. 1. Develop my own model and validate on the external dataset? 2. Combine the entire dataset for modelling and then use bootstrapping for validation to get optimism correction for the model evaluation criteria? First, I recommend the paper by Steyerberg and Harrell It gives the answer - both internal validation and external. If some of your candidate predictors are ordinal, or you need to use splines for your continuous variables then you will have a lot of degrees of freedom (more than 10) which will require more events. Checking both predictive performance and calibration in an external validation data set is key. I’ve seen where the gross discrimination metrics look good, but calibration is poor - meaning re-calibration likely necessary (one can also, then, make a model using all the data). I could try to use the internal external cross validation in the model development phase. * A practical problem might be that some centers being big and others small, different runs of the cross validation might have different sample sizes and therefore the results may be confusing. * What is essentially the benefit of taking this approach instead of taking all the cases in model development and using the center (or its treatment pattern) as a covariate? If I do center by center cross validation I will get more variability in my metrics, but if I can just combine the cases and use these factors as covariates with a larger sample size and just do bootstrapping, how much do I lose out? Especially so since my final model after internal external cross validation will include data from all centers anyway. Browse other topics in model validation or view latest topics.

results.title: Determine provider-level sample sizes for patient satisfaction surveys
results.content: When conducting survey research there will always be sampling errors, a term that refers to the differences between survey results from a sample and potential results achieved if every patient in the panel responded to the survey.2 Obtaining responses from every patient in the panel is generally not feasible, which is one reason why results can be thought of as estimates of potential results or true population values. * Determine how many survey responses (per provider) are necessary to stay within a desired margin of error. * Consider the minimum number of survey responses necessary to stay within your margin of error and the average response rate for your survey distribution method to determine an appropriate per provider sample size. The table below provides the minimum number of survey responses required to achieve specific margins of error. Note that a minimum of 50 survey responses are necessary (per provider) to stay within a 14% margin of error. When defining an appropriate sample size, the minimum number of survey responses necessary to stay within the predetermined margin of error and the average response rate for a given survey distribution method must both be considered. An appropriate provider sample size (i.e., the number of surveys to distribute per provider) can be determined using these average response rates and the minimum number of survey responses needed to stay within a maximum margin of error. The table below provides sample size recommendations based on margins of error and survey distribution methods. If your response rate is lower than average for mailed surveys, the 50 responses necessary to stay within a 14% margin of error might not be received. If you achieve an average response rate for your survey distribution method, you will maintain this moderate margin of error that is less than the industry standard of 14%. Additionally, the larger sample sizes associated with 10% and 12% margins of error provide some insurance against dropping below the industry standard of 50 responses per provider or the minimum requirement of 30 responses per provider in case of lower than average response rates.

results.content: # **Asthma Control Assessment: To ACT, ACQ, or AIRQ?**. ### Asthma Control Assessment: To ACT, ACQ, or AIRQ? **Asthma Control Assessment: To ACT, ACQ, or AIRQ?**. And even though there are tools available like the Asthma Control Test (ACT) and the Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ), assessing asthma control has been overestimated by patients, physicians, and caregivers alike. **Similarities and Differences Between Asthma Control Assessments**. The ACT and ACQ have been widely used in clinical practice and research to assess asthma control, while the AIRQ is an emerging tool. A summary of common tools to assess asthma control appears in Table 1 below. Other research found that neither the ACT nor the ACQ is useful for the assessment of uncontrolled asthma. **ACT:** The ACT has diagnostic accuracy for the assessment of controlled asthma. **ACQ:** The ACQ is diagnostically accurate for assessing not well-controlled asthma at prespecified cutoff points. Like the ACT, however, it lacks assessment of risk of future asthma exacerbations. Summary of Asthma Control Assessment Tools. The use of tools like the AIRQ, ACT, and ACQ can have a significant impact on patient care as it enables healthcare providers to effectively identify patients who are at risk. The place of the AIRQ in assessing asthma is yet to be determined, but findings suggest that the AIRQ is a valid tool for assessing asthma control and can provide useful information regarding patient perception of disease status, health-related quality of life, and treatment adherence. results.title: What are Survey Sample Sizes & How to Find Your Sample Size
results.content: One of the key components of an effective surveys is your sample size — the group you are trying to gather data about. + What Are Survey Sample Sizes? ## What Are Survey Sample Sizes? A survey sample size refers to the number of participants you have in a study because it's not usually possible to gather responses from an entire target group. ### **What is a good sample size for a survey?**. Essentially, your sample size is decided based on the population, how confident you want to be in your results, and the margin of error you‘d like to allow for. Below, I used a sample size calculator and I put in that my population size is 10,000, and I'd like to be 95% confident in my results within a 5% margin of error. **Pro tip:** Remember to focus on both the sample size for the survey as well as the sample for a specific stat you’re looking for, explains Jessica Davis, Senior Manager of Customer Insights Marketing at HubSpot. Kristie (Kay) Savage, head of Fanatics, Inc.’s Gaming Group’s Data Science and Product + Customer Data Program, breaks this down a little more in-depth: “When administering a survey about sentiment, attitudes, and/or behaviors, you can calculate your sample size based on your population and tolerance for error. “These numbers were calculated using a formula, and there are many online calculators dedicated to helping you find your sample size for surveys, based on two factors: population size and tolerance for error. In fact, an even more conservative approach would be to account for a 10-15% response rate, meaning you should send your survey to many more people than the required sample size to ensure you receive that many responses. Since this step requires you to estimate how the responses to your survey will vary, you’ll want to pick a standard deviation of .5 to ensure your sample size is large enough. If your sample size is too large, you can make adjustments by increasing your margin of error or decreasing your confidence level. It’s a great way to remain representative and catch changes in opinion, even if the group’s small — you’re getting accurate, changing feedback without having a big sample size.”.
